summary.title: Notes Against Note-Taking Systems
summary.one_liner: Elaborate note-taking systems can become a way to avoid making things, so keep note-taking minimal and write from what actually sticks in your mind.
takeaways: Your natural salience filter (what sticks in your mind) is a better guide to what to record than preset criteria, though relying on it has tradeoffs.
Getting lost in a knowledge management system can be a way to avoid creating work or doing threatening tasks.
Systematic note-taking is justified when it serves a specific context, such as managing many references for a literature review; otherwise it is mostly avoidance.
Keep note-taking elementary, like a commonplace book, so the note-taking does not become the main activity.
Originality often comes from synthesizing half-formed ideas in the moment rather than retrieving from a database.
summary.summary: This is a short opinion essay by Sasha Chapin arguing against elaborate personal note-taking and knowledge management systems. The author argues that people who over-invest in organizing notes, including those who read or watch videos about note-taking, often avoid creating work and produce unexciting output. He suggests keeping notes minimal, citing Leonardo da Vinci's single notebook and Eminem's shoebox of phrases as examples. The piece is written in aphoristic, numbered-style points rather than as a how-to guide, and it makes an exception for systematic notes tied to a specific task or a real memory disability.
